ethics.disclaimer: KindTrail is an independent UK training guidance product. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Institute of Modern Dog Trainers (IMDT Ltd). Content is paraphrased from registered sources in our research knowledge base.

safetyRules.title: Do not recommend pain, fear or coercion as routine training
safetyRules.rule: Good Dog must not present pain, intimidation, choke chains, shouting, hitting, or aversive equipment as standard training solutions.
safetyRules.referralText: Direct owner to reward-based professional (ABTC/IMDT-aligned) if current trainer uses aversives.

safetyRules.title: Manage recall failure with lines and secure areas
safetyRules.rule: Until recall is reliable, keep the dog on a long line or lead; off-lead only in secure areas or when confidence in recall is established.
safetyRules.referralText: If recall does not improve, refer to qualified trainer or behaviourist.

safetyRules.title: Never punish a dog for coming back late
safetyRules.rule: After recall, even if slow, use positive reinforcement; avoid anger, shouting, or ending fun as punishment for late return.

safetyRules.title: Refer beyond training education scope
safetyRules.rule: Aggression, severe fear, sudden unexplained behaviour change, or suspected pain/illness require veterinary and/or clinical behaviour referral—not generic app protocols alone.
safetyRules.referralText: Contact veterinarian for medical causes; seek ABTC-registered Clinical Animal Behaviourist or Veterinary Behaviourist for clinical behaviour treatment.

safetyRules.title: Do not punish warning signals without addressing cause
safetyRules.rule: Do not train owners to suppress growling or other warnings without addressing underlying fear, pain, or conflict; prioritise management and professional support.

safetyRules.title: Always supervise children and dogs
safetyRules.rule: Never leave a child alone with a dog; teach do-not-disturb contexts and gentle interaction.

safetyRules.title: Do not punish warning signals
safetyRules.rule: Do not punish growling or other warnings; remove dog from trigger and seek vet/behaviourist support.
safetyRules.referralText: Veterinary assessment and accredited animal behaviourist.

safetyRules.title: Do not recommend ABTC-listed aversive tools or methods
safetyRules.rule: Good Dog must not recommend equipment or methods on ABTC indicative aversive lists (e.g. shock, choke, prong, alpha roll).

supportingClaims.statement: IMDT members agree to actively provide and promote force-free training methods and reject methods or equipment that may cause physical or mental discomfort.
IMDT members agree to avoid positive punishment and negative reinforcement as tools for training dogs.
IMDT members agree to work within professional limits and refer owners to a suitable professional when needs exceed those limits.
ABTC states it does not agree with aversives being used to train animals and publishes an indicative list of aversive equipment and methods that should not be used.
If a dog ignores recall during training, Dogs Trust advises staying calm because anger or shouting can reduce willingness to return; use long line guidance or collect the dog instead of punishing.
Dogs Trust advises off-lead exercise in open spaces only when the owner is confident the dog will come back when called.
RSPCA advises owners not to join classes if techniques rely on fear, pain, choke chains, shouting or hitting.
If a dog does not always come when called, Dogs Trust advises keeping them on a long line or lead rather than relying on off-lead freedom.
RSPCA advises never leaving a child alone in the same room as a dog, even the family dog.
RSPCA advises teaching children not to approach dogs when the dog is eating, sleeping, unwell, injured, tired, or near valued items.
Blue Cross advises not punishing dogs showing defensive behaviours such as growling, because punishment may suppress warnings and increase biting risk while adding stress.
Blue Cross advises removing the dog from a worrying situation when stress signs appear (e.g. lip lick, growl, moving away) and giving a calming activity such as a chew or stuffed Kong.
ABTC's June 2024 indicative list includes electric/shock collars, choke chains/collars, and prong/pinch collars as aversive equipment that should not be used in training animals.
ABTC's indicative aversive methods list includes 'alpha roll'/pinning, hitting, hard lead jerks, and kneeing the dog as methods that should not be used.
Dogs Trust immediate reactivity guidance: increase distance until the dog relaxes, then reward with praise, food or a favourite toy; avoid telling the dog off because this can increase stress.

abtcRegister.title: Find an ABTC-registered trainer
abtcRegister.body: RSPCA recommends looking for ABTC-registered animal training instructors for ethical training that meets welfare needs.

vetFirst.title: See your vet first
vetFirst.body: Dogs Trust advises having a reactive dog examined by a vet to check for underlying medical conditions before behaviour change work, noting pain and illness can reduce tolerance and coping.

dogsTrustBehaviourLine.title: Dogs Trust Behaviour Support Line
dogsTrustBehaviourLine.body: Free telephone advice for UK dog owners struggling with behaviour.

lesson.title: Introduce a marker word
lesson.summary: Teach your dog that a calm 'yes' (or click) always means a reward is coming, before learning new skills.

protocol.title: Charge a marker signal (Dogs Trust pattern)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog shows clear anticipation (orientation toward handler/treats) immediately after marker with no behaviour requirement.

steps.instruction: Choose one marker (calm verbal word such as 'yes', clicker, whistle, or visual signal for deaf dogs) and use it consistently in tone and form.
steps.rewardTiming: Deliver treat immediately after each marker.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog orients toward handler or treats within one second of marker on repeated trials.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use higher-value treats; reduce environmental stimulation; increase distance from distractions.
failureModes: Marker word used in daily speech causing confusion

steps.instruction: Repeat marker then treat pairing multiple times in a short session until dog visibly anticipates food after the marker alone.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat within 1–2 seconds of marker on every repetition during charging phase.
steps.progressCriteria: Anticipatory response to marker without requiring body movement cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten sessions; pause if dog disengages.
failureModes: Gaps between marker and treat too long

steps.instruction: Begin teaching new behaviours only after charging criterion met; maintain rule that marker is always followed by reward during learning phase.
steps.rewardTiming: Marker marks exact behaviour instant; reward follows immediately.
steps.progressCriteria: Stable anticipation across at least two sessions.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Re-charge marker in easier environment if anticipation fades.

safetyPrecautions: Do not train on full stomach if dog prone to vomiting with excitement—adjust timing

claims.statement: A marker signal must always be followed by a reward so the dog can be confident they got the behaviour right.
Before training new behaviours, the dog should learn that the marker predicts a reward via repeated marker-then-treat pairings.
Dogs Trust advises saying a verbal marker as calmly as possible because excited delivery can excite, confuse or distract the dog.

sources.title: How to introduce a marker to your dog training

lesson.title: First sit with a lure
lesson.summary: Use a treat lure, reward the moment your dog sits, then add the word 'sit' at the right time.

protocol.title: Teach sit with food lure (RSPCA six-step outline)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog sits on verbal cue 'sit' with hindquarters on ground.

steps.instruction: With dog standing, hold treat near nose.
steps.rewardTiming: No reward until sit occurs in later steps.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog tracks treat with nose.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use smellier treat; shorten sessions.
failureModes: Lure held too high causing jump

steps.instruction: Move hand in arc over head so dog follows treat; as head rises, bottom goes to floor; praise and treat the instant sit happens.
steps.progressCriteria: Bottom contacts floor following lure arc.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Smaller arc; reward partial sits only if shaping intentionally.
failureModes: Backing up instead of sitting—train with wall behind

steps.instruction: Practice in short regular sessions.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat each successful sit during acquisition.
steps.progressCriteria: Repeated sits with lure.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Fewer reps per session.

steps.instruction: Add verbal cue 'sit' as dog moves into sit, not before movement.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat on completed sit after cue timed correctly.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog sits when lure used with correctly timed verbal cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Delay adding verbal cue until lure reliable.

steps.instruction: Continue short regular practice.
steps.progressCriteria: Sit begins without excessive lure dependence.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Fade lure gradually—not specified numerically by RSPCA.

steps.instruction: Use an 'okay' or release cue to mark end of exercise.
steps.rewardTiming: Optional release reward per owner choice.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog waits until release after sit when trained for duration separately.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Keep duration short initially.

claims.statement: RSPCA recommends breaking training into short but regular sessions and starting new tricks in a quiet room with minimal distractions.
RSPCA advises adding the verbal cue 'sit' only as the dog moves into sit, not before, to avoid associating the word with the wrong movement.

sources.title: How to train a dog to sit — RSPCA

lesson.title: Teach down without forcing
lesson.summary: Lure or shape a down and never push your dog into position.

protocol.title: Lie down with lure and shaping (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog lies down on verbal 'down' cue.

steps.instruction: From sit, lure hand toward floor in front of paws; mark and reward any down or shaping step toward floor.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark at elbows on floor or closest approximation.
steps.progressCriteria: Full down with lure.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reward head dip or elbow bend only until full down emerges.

steps.instruction: Fade visible lure; add verbal 'down' before gesture once behaviour reliable.
steps.progressCriteria: Down on verbal cue with minimal gesture.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reintroduce brief lure.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust instructs owners never to push a dog's back down to force a down; use luring/shaping and reward instead.
If a dog does not fully lie down initially, Dogs Trust advises marking and rewarding incremental movements toward the floor (head lower, bend) before requiring a full down.

sources.title: How to train your dog to lie down

lesson.title: Build name response
lesson.summary: Reward check-ins, then teach your dog that their name means look at you—without repeating it.

protocol.title: Name response and attention (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog orients to handler promptly when name is spoken once.

steps.instruction: Reward every voluntary glance toward handler without saying name yet.
steps.progressCriteria: Frequent check-ins.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Higher value treats.
failureModes: Only rewarding when dog is naughty

steps.instruction: Say name once; when dog looks, throw treat to side; repeat varying direction; generalise locations.
steps.progressCriteria: Reliable name response in moderate distraction.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Do not repeat name; move slightly to prompt.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust recommends rewarding every glance the dog gives the handler during early focus training before adding the name cue.
Dogs Trust advises not repeating the dog's name rapidly if they fail to respond, to avoid teaching the dog to ignore it.

sources.title: How to teach your dog their name (full extraction)

lesson.title: Settle on a mat
lesson.summary: Help your dog choose calm on a blanket, with more relaxation rewarded over time.

protocol.title: Settle on mat (Dogs Trust relaxation training)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog voluntarily relaxes on blanket/mat with increasing duration and distractions.

steps.instruction: Sit quietly; drop treats on mat for any behaviour that is not staring, pulling, or barking; gradually reinforce lie down and relaxation signs.
steps.rewardTiming: Quiet delivery of treats onto mat.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog chooses mat and shows relaxed posture.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reward standing quietly or sniffing blanket first.
failureModes: Talking or commanding repeatedly during settle

steps.instruction: Increase duration between treats; add distractions at distance; if dog gets up, wait for re-settle before rewarding.
steps.progressCriteria: Settle with mild distractions indoors/outdoors.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase distance from distraction.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust settle training aims for the dog to choose calm, relaxed behaviour without the owner repeatedly instructing them during the exercise.
Dogs Trust advises progressively rewarding more relaxed behaviours (lying down, sighing, weight shift, head rest) during settle training on a blanket or mat.

sources.title: How to train your dog to be calm, relax and settle

lesson.title: Leave it — foundations
lesson.summary: Teach your dog to look away from tempting items and wait for a better reward.

protocol.title: Leave it — look away progression (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog orientates away from presented item on 'leave' cue without taking it.

steps.instruction: Hold low-value item in one hand; when dog sniffs then looks or moves away, mark and reward from other hand with better treat.
steps.progressCriteria: Reliable look-away before cue added.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use more boring decoy item; higher-value reward.

steps.instruction: Add verbal cue 'leave' as item presented; mark and reward look-away.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog looks away on cue before item reachable.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase distance to item.

steps.instruction: Generalise: new locations, item on floor, dropped from low height, gradually higher-value forbidden items.
steps.rewardTiming: Maintain high-value reward for difficult leaves.
steps.progressCriteria: Success in moderate distraction environments.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Return to earlier step per Dogs Trust guidance.
failureModes: Progressing value or distraction too fast

referralRequirements: Persistent failure to leave—training classes or behaviourist
safetyPrecautions: Use fair trade instead of force-taking items from mouth

claims.statement: Dogs Trust recommends swapping items a dog should not have for something better ('fair trade') so the dog willingly releases items rather than guarding them.
To teach 'leave it', Dogs Trust advises waiting for the dog to look or move away from a low-value item, then marking and rewarding with a higher-value treat from the other hand.

sources.title: How to train your dog to leave it

lesson.title: Teach leave (RSPCA method)
lesson.summary: Reward your dog for backing away from something so leaving it feels safe and worthwhile.

protocol.title: Leave — fist closed progression (RSPCA)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog disengages from presented item on gentle 'leave' cue.

steps.instruction: Place treat in closed fist; say 'take it' in friendly voice and let dog sniff/lick closed hand without opening.
steps.rewardTiming: No reward until dog backs off.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog learns closed fist does not release on mouthing.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use lower-value treat in fist; higher-value reward when opening hand.
failureModes: Opening fist while dog is mouthing

steps.instruction: When dog backs off even slightly, open fist, release treat and praise generously.
steps.progressCriteria: Consistent back-off before treat release.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Wait for larger gap if needed.
failureModes: Rewarding while nose still on fist

steps.instruction: Add gentle 'leave' as dog backs off, then release treat; progress to treat visible in open palm and reward from other hand when dog leaves it.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat from other hand after successful leave.
steps.progressCriteria: Leaves visible palm item on cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Close hand if dog moves toward palm treat.

safetyPrecautions: Pair with fair-trade if item already in mouth (see Dogs Trust leave guidance)

claims.statement: RSPCA teaches 'leave' by waiting for the dog to back off from a treat in a closed fist, then opening the hand to release the treat and praise—building that disengaging is rewarded.
RSPCA instructs adding the cue word 'leave' in a gentle tone as the dog backs off, before releasing the treat.

sources.title: How to train your dog to leave something alone — RSPCA

lesson.title: Stop when the lead tightens
lesson.summary: Help your dog learn that a loose lead keeps the walk moving.

protocol.title: Loose-lead walking — stop-start method (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog walks with slack lead; forward motion contingent on loose lead.

steps.instruction: Reward dog for standing/sitting at handler side without lead; add lead when reliable.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog chooses proximity without pulling.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Higher-value rewards; quieter location.

steps.instruction: When lead tightens, stop immediately; remain quiet until slack, then move forward.
steps.rewardTiming: Forward motion is reinforcer; optional treats at side.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog orients back and loosens lead to restart walk.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Walk opposite direction briefly to regain focus.

steps.instruction: Maintain consistency each walk; expect longer walks during learning phase.
steps.progressCriteria: Slack lead maintained with moderate distractions.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reduce distractions; shorten sessions.

safetyPrecautions: Do not use pain-based anti-pull devices per Dogs Trust and ABTC lists

claims.statement: Dogs Trust teaches that when the lead tightens, the handler stops walking and does not move forward until the lead is slack again.

Dogs Trust states that equipment promising to 'cure' pulling by causing pain or discomfort in sensitive areas is unnecessary and can be unpleasant and confusing for dogs; flat collar or comfortable harness is preferred.

sources.title: Teach your dog to walk nicely on a lead

lesson.title: Socialise your puppy safely
lesson.summary: Go at your puppy's pace, keep experiences positive, and follow your vet's guidance before walks on the ground.

protocol.title: Puppy socialisation — positive exposure checklist (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Puppy forms positive associations with everyday people, animals, sounds, surfaces and objects during the early socialisation window.

steps.instruction: Begin at home with gentle handling, household sounds (e.g. vacuum off then on at distance), varied surfaces and props (hats, umbrellas) at puppy's pace with rewards for relaxed behaviour.
steps.progressCriteria: Puppy accepts novel home stimuli without fleeing.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase distance; reduce duration; split stimuli.

steps.instruction: Before full vaccination, carry puppy to observe people, traffic and dogs from safe distance; reward calm observation.
steps.progressCriteria: Calm observation at sub-threshold distances.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorter outings; quieter locations.

steps.instruction: After vaccination clearance, introduce walks, varied dogs/animals at distance, visitors and sound desensitisation; stop immediately if puppy becomes worried or over-aroused.
steps.progressCriteria: Growing confidence across checklist categories without shutdown.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Return to earlier step; consult vet/trainer.

referralRequirements: Puppy class with reward-based ABTC instructor optional
safetyPrecautions: Follow vet vaccination and parasite advice

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states the first four months are a vital socialisation window when puppies learn what is normal, requiring gradual positive introductions to people, dogs, noises, objects and experiences.

Dogs Trust advises puppies should not walk on public ground before full vaccination, but can be carried (carrier/sling) to begin socialisation experiences until the vet confirms it is safe to go on the ground.

Dogs Trust instructs stopping socialisation interactions immediately if the puppy shows high arousal or signs of becoming worried or frightened, because negative or overwhelming early experiences increase later behaviour problems.
Dogs Trust Puppy 101 hub advises going at the individual puppy's pace and using rewards they like for kind, positive learning rather than a one-size-fits-all checklist.
